title: Body and health
goal: Say what hurts, buy medicine, and ask for help — using the sentence pattern Estonian keeps especially for pain.
bekal: name the most common body parts and symptoms
form commands for one person and for someone you address politely

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Apteegis
dialogs.intro: November. Budi walks into a pharmacy with a hoarse voice.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma ei tea. Mul on külm ja ma olen väsinud.
lines.id: I don't know. I'm cold and tired.
lines.literal: I not know. me-at is cold and I am-I tired.

lines.speaker: Apteeker:
lines.text: See on tavaline külmetus. Siin on ravim.
lines.id: It's an ordinary cold. Here's the medicine.
lines.literal: it is-it ordinary cold. here is medicine.

lines.speaker: Apteeker:
lines.id: Two tablets a day, after meals.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aitäh. Kas ma pean arsti juurde minema?
lines.id: Thanks. Should I see a doctor?
lines.literal: thanks. question I must-I doctor-gen to-place to-go?

lines.speaker: Apteeker:
lines.text: Kui palavik ei lange kolme päevaga, siis jah.
lines.id: If the fever doesn't go down in three days, yes.
lines.literal: if fever not drop-it three day-with, then yes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Got it. And in an emergency?

lines.speaker: Apteeker:
lines.text: Helistage 112. See on tasuta ja töötab alati.
lines.id: Call 112. It's free and always works.
lines.literal: call 112. it is-it free and works-it always.

notes: ⚠️ **Mul valutab pea** — literally "at me hurts the head". The thing that hurts becomes the **subject**, and its owner is marked with the ending **-l**. This pattern is used for all pain: *mul valutab kõht* (my stomach hurts), *tal valutab hammas* (his/her tooth hurts).
**Mul on külm** means "I'm cold", not "I have cold". The pattern *mul on* + adjective covers many physical states: *mul on soe* (I'm hot), *mul on igav* (I'm bored), *mul on hea meel* (I'm glad).
**Mis teil viga on?** — the standard question from pharmacists and doctors, literally "what flaw is at you". Don't be offended; it's completely neutral.
⚠️ **112 is the emergency number for all of Estonia** — ambulance, fire and police in one. Free from any phone, including one with no credit, and the operators speak English. Save it now.

grammars.title: Three ways to say it hurts
body: All three are correct. The difference is how precisely you can point to where it hurts.

head: Pattern
Example
English
When
rows: Pain without pointing to a place.
Not sure what it is yet.

after: ⚠️ Notice that **none of them uses a possessive**. Estonian doesn't say "my head hurts" with *minu pea*; it says *mul valutab pea* — "at me, the head hurts". The *-l* ending already takes care of ownership.
To ask: *Kus valutab?* (Where does it hurt?) or *Mis viga?* (What's wrong?). Both are very common.
*Valus* is also used as an adjective: *valus hammas* (a sore tooth), *valus koht* (a sore spot).

grammars.title: Commands — and their shortcut
body: You've been using them since unit 7 (*tule sisse*, *kuula*) and unit 15 (*minge*, *võtke*). Here's the rule, and it comes with a pleasant shortcut.
after: ⚠️ **The shortcut: the command form for *sa* is exactly the form used after *ei*.** *Ei mine* and *mine!* use the same form. So the rule from unit 11 — take the *ma* form, drop the *-n* — also gives you every command form. One rule, two jobs.
The *te* form is made by adding **-ke** or **-ge**. It's used with people you address politely, with strangers, and with more than one person.
To say "let's", use the *me* form without the pronoun: *lähme!* (let's go), *sööme!* (let's eat), *vaatame!* (let's see). You've been using it since unit 7.

blocks.text: You've already seen many of these in the list of pairs in unit 6 — *jalg – jala*, *käsi – käe*, *selg – selja*, *nägu – näo*. Body parts are among the oldest words in a language, and the oldest words are the ones that change the most.
⚠️ *Süda* means **heart** both as an organ and as feelings, exactly like English "heart". *Mul on hea süda* — I have a good heart.

blocks.title: Sentences you need to have ready now
items: *Ma vajan arsti.* — I need a doctor.
*Palun kutsuge kiirabi!* — Please call an ambulance!
⚠️ **112** — the emergency number for ambulance, fire and police. Free, available twenty-four hours a day, and the operators speak English.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Terviseks does three jobs
items: **When toasting** — *Terviseks!* means "to health", the equivalent of "cheers".
**As a general good wish** — said when parting from someone who is ill.
The root word is *tervis* (health) — the same root as the greeting *tervist!* you learned in unit 1.
